title: King Asks Wrong 'God', Gets Literally Roasted

paragraphs: Alright, so after King Ahab died, the whole nation of Moab decided they were done with Israel and started a rebellion.

So, the new king, Ahaziah, was hanging out at his palace in Samaria when he lost his footing and fell through the balcony railing on his roof. It was a pretty bad injury. Instead of asking God for help, he sent his messengers to go ask this idol, Baal-Zebub, the god of a town called Ekron, 'Am I gonna pull through this?'

But an angel of God spoke to Elijah the Tishbite and said, 'Hey, get up and go meet the king of Samaria's messengers.' The angel told him to give them this message: 'What's the deal? Is it because there's no God in Israel that you guys are running off to consult Baal-Zebub, god of Ekron? Here's the real message from the God you're trying to ignore: You're not getting out of that bed. You're as good as dead.' So Elijah delivered the message and was gone.
The messengers went straight back to the king. He was like, 'Wait, why are you back so soon? What happened?'

They told him, 'This random guy met us and told us to turn back and tell you a message from God. He said, "Is it because there's no God in Israel that you're sending people to consult Baal-Zebub, god of Ekron? You needn't bother. You're not getting out of that bed you're in—you're toast."'
The king asked, 'Hold on, describe this guy who met you and said all this. What did he look like?'
'He was a pretty rugged dude,' they said, 'all hairy and wearing a leather belt.'
'Yup, that's Elijah the Tishbite,' the king said. He knew exactly who it was.
So the king sent a captain with fifty soldiers to get Elijah. Elijah was just chilling on top of a hill. The captain went up and said, 'O Holy Man! The king orders you to come down!'
Elijah shot back, 'If I'm really a 'holy man,' then let fire come down from the sky and burn you and your fifty men.' And BAM! Lightning zapped the captain and his whole crew.
The king, not getting the hint, sent another captain with another fifty men. This guy also went up and said, 'O Holy Man! The king's orders are for you to come down, like, right now!'
Elijah replied, 'If I'm a 'holy man,' let fire come down and get you and your fifty men.' And boom, another lightning strike from God toasted that captain and his guys too.

Seriously, the king sent a THIRD captain with fifty more men. But this captain was smart. He went up, fell on his knees, and begged, 'O Holy Man, please, have mercy on me and my men! I know lightning has already fried two other captains and their crews. Please, I'm begging you, spare my life!'
Then the angel of God told Elijah, 'Go ahead, go with him. Don't be afraid.' So Elijah got up and went with the captain to see the king.

Elijah went right up to the king and said, 'Here's God's word: Because you sent messengers to consult Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron, as if there's no God in Israel to pray to, you will never get out of that bed. You're already as good as dead.'
And just like that, he died, exactly as God had said through Elijah.
Since Ahaziah didn't have a son, his brother Joram became the next king. This all happened in the second year that Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, was king of Judah.
And that's the story of Ahaziah. The rest of his life is written down in the official records of the kings of Israel.

title: Elijah's Epic Exit & Elisha's Wild First Day
paragraphs: Just before God took Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were walking from Gilgal. Elijah told Elisha, “Hey, you should probably stay here. God’s sending me to Bethel on an errand.”
But Elisha said, “As God lives and you live, I’m not leaving you.” So they went to Bethel together.
The squad of prophets at Bethel came up to Elisha and asked, “Bro, did you know God is taking your master from you today?”
He was like, “Yeah, I know. But let’s keep it lowkey.”
Then Elijah said, “Stay here. God’s sending me to Jericho.”
Elisha shot back, “Not a chance. As God lives and you live, I’m not leaving you.” So they went to Jericho together.
The prophet squad at Jericho came to Elisha and said, “You know God’s about to take your master from you today, right?”
He said, “Yeah, I know. Just be cool about it.”
Then Elijah said, “Stay here. God’s sending me to the Jordan River.”
Elisha said, “Nope. As God lives and you live, I’m not leaving.” So the two of them kept going.
Meanwhile, fifty guys from the prophet squad were watching from a distance as the two of them stood by the Jordan.
Elijah took off his cloak, rolled it up, and smacked the water with it. The water split down the middle, and the two of them walked across on dry ground. It was wild.
When they got to the other side, Elijah asked Elisha, “Alright, what can I do for you before I’m taken away? Ask for anything.”
Elisha said, “I want a double portion of your spirit. I want to be a man of God just like you.”
Elijah said, “That’s a tough one. But if you see me when I’m taken from you, you’ll get it. But only if you’re watching.”

And then it happened. As they were walking and talking, a chariot of fire with horses of fire suddenly appeared between them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha saw it all and screamed, “My father, my father! The chariot and horsemen of Israel!” And then he couldn’t see him anymore. He grabbed his own clothes and ripped them in two.

Then he picked up Elijah’s cloak that had fallen, went back to the bank of the Jordan, and stood there. He took the cloak and hit the water with it, saying, “Where is the God of Elijah now? Where is he?”
When he hit the water, it divided, and Elisha walked across.
The prophet squad from Jericho saw the whole thing from a distance and said, “Whoa, the spirit of Elijah is on Elisha now!” They came to meet him and bowed down.
They said to him, “Look, we’ve got fifty strong guys here. Let us go and search for your master. Maybe the Spirit of God dropped him on a mountain or in a valley somewhere.”
Elisha said, “No. Don’t send them.”
But they pestered him until he gave in: “Fine. Go ahead, send them.”
So they sent the fifty men, and for three days they searched high and low, but found nothing.
When they came back to Elisha in Jericho, he said, “See? Told you so.”
The men of the city came to Elisha and said, “Master, this city is in a nice spot, but the water is bad, and it’s causing our crops to fail.”
He said, “Bring me a new bowl and put some salt in it.” They brought it to him.

He went to the spring, sprinkled the salt into it, and proclaimed, “This is what God says: ‘I have healed this water. It won’t cause death or make the land unproductive anymore.’” And the water has been pure ever since, just like Elisha said.
Another time, Elisha was walking up to Bethel, and a bunch of kids from the town came out and started making fun of him, yelling, “Go on up, baldy! Go on up, baldy!”
Elisha turned around, took one look at them, and cursed them in the name of God. Then two bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of those kids.
Elisha then went on to Mount Carmel and later returned to Samaria.

title: The Time God Sent a Flood Without Rain
paragraphs: So, Joram, Ahab's son, became the king of Israel in Samaria. This was during the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat's rule in Judah. He was king for twelve years, and honestly, he was a pretty bad king in God's eyes. But he wasn't as bad as his mom and dad. To his credit, he did get rid of the messed-up Baal statue his dad had made. But he was still into the same sinful stuff as Jeroboam son of Nebat, whose sins had corrupted Israel for a long time. He just wouldn't quit.

Now, King Mesha of Moab was a sheep guy. He was forced to give the king of Israel 100,000 lambs and 100,000 rams. But when Ahab died, the king of Moab was like, 'I'm out,' and rebelled against the king of Israel. So King Joram set out from Samaria and got his army ready for war. First thing he did was send a message to Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, saying, 'The king of Moab is rebelling against me. You wanna join me and fight him?'
Jehoshaphat was all in. 'I'm with you, man. My soldiers are your soldiers, my horses are your horses. Which way are we going?'
'Through the desert of Edom.'
So the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom started out on this crazy, long detour. After seven days, they ran out of water for both the army and the animals.
The king of Israel was like, 'This is bad. God brought us three kings out here just to let Moab destroy us.'

But Jehoshaphat asked, 'Isn't there a prophet of God around here we can ask?' One of the servants of the king of Israel said, 'Elisha son of Shaphat is around somewhere—the one who was Elijah's right-hand man.'
One of the king of Israel's servants said, 'Elisha son of Shaphat is somewhere around here—he was Elijah's right-hand man.'
Jehoshaphat said, 'Perfect! A guy we can trust!' So the three kings—Israel, Jehoshaphat, and Edom—went to find him.
Elisha looked at the king of Israel and said, 'What do you want from me? Go ask the fake prophets your parents listened to.'
'No way!' said the king of Israel. 'It's God who got us into this mess, and now he's going to let Moab defeat all three of us.'

Elisha said, 'As the God of Angel Armies lives, the one I serve, if it wasn't for the respect I have for King Jehoshaphat of Judah, I wouldn't even be talking to you. But since you're here, bring me a musician.' (When the musician played, the power of God came on Elisha.)

Then he said, 'God's word: Dig ditches all over this valley. And here's what's gonna happen—you won't hear any wind, you won't see any rain, but this valley is going to fill up with water, and your army and animals will have plenty to drink. This is easy for God to do; he's also going to give you victory over Moab. You will ravage their country: take out its fortifications, flatten the key villages, cut down the orchards, clog the springs, and litter the cultivated fields with rocks.'
In the morning, around the time of the morning sacrifice, water started pouring in from the west, from Edom. It was a flash flood that filled the whole valley.

By this time, everyone in Moab had heard that the kings were coming to fight them. Every guy who could hold a sword was called up and they all stood at the border. They were up early in the morning when the sun rose over the water. From where the Moabites were standing, the water looked red, like blood.
'Blood! Look at the blood!' they said. 'The kings must have fought each other—a total massacre! Let's go get the loot, Moab!'

When Moab entered the Israelite camp, the Israelites jumped up and started attacking them. The Moabites ran for their lives, but the Israelites were relentless—it was a slaughter. They destroyed the towns, covered the fields with rocks, blocked the springs, and cut down the orchards. Only the capital city, Kir Hareseth, was left, and not for long. It was surrounded and attacked with slingshots and rocks.

When the king of Moab saw that he was losing, he took seven hundred swordsmen to try and break through the king of Edom's line, but they failed. Then he took his oldest son, the one who was supposed to be the next king, and sacrificed him on the city wall. This set off furious anger against Israel. So Israel pulled back and went home.

title: Prophet's Miracles Go VIRAL
paragraphs: So, the wife of a guy from the prophet squad went to Elisha and was like, “My husband, your student, is dead. You know he was a solid dude who was all in for God. But now, the guy he owed money to is coming to take my two sons as slaves to settle the debt.”
Elisha said, “Okay, how can I help? Tell me, what do you have in your house?”
“Literally nothing,” she said. “Well, except for a tiny bit of oil.”

“Alright, here’s the game plan,” Elisha said. “Go ask all your neighbors and borrow every empty jar and container you can find. And I mean a LOT—get as many as possible. Then go home, lock the door with you and your sons inside. Start pouring that little bit of oil into every container. When one’s full, put it to the side and grab the next one.”

She did exactly what he said. She locked the door with her and her sons inside. They kept bringing her containers, and she kept filling them up. When every single jar and bowl was full, she asked one of her sons, “Hey, pass me another jar.”
He replied, “That’s it. There are no more.”
And just like that, the oil stopped flowing.
She went and told the man of God what happened. He said, “Go sell all that oil and pay off your debts. You and your sons can live on the money that’s left over.”

Another time, Elisha was passing through a town called Shunem. A really important woman in the town convinced him to stop and have a meal. After that, it became a thing: whenever he was in the area, he’d stop by her place to eat.

The woman told her husband, “I’m pretty sure this guy who always stops by is a holy man of God. What if we build a small room for him on the roof? We can put a bed, a desk, a chair, and a lamp in it. That way, whenever he comes, he has his own space to crash.”
So, it happened. The next time Elisha came, he went up to his new room and took a nap.
He told his servant, Gehazi, “Go tell the Shunammite woman I want to talk to her.” So Gehazi called her, and she came up.
Elisha had Gehazi tell her, “You’ve done so much for us, way more than you had to. What can we do for you? You want us to put in a good word for you with the king or the army commander?”
She was like, “Nah, I’m good. I’ve got my family, I’m content.”
Elisha talked it over with Gehazi, “There has to be something we can do for her. But what?”
Gehazi said, “Well, she doesn’t have a son, and her husband is pretty old.”
“Call her back,” Elisha said. He called her, and she stood at the doorway.
Elisha told her, “A year from now, you’re going to be holding your own baby boy.”
She was like, “Whoa, master, man of God, for real? Don’t play with me like that. Don’t get my hopes up with some fantasy.”
But the woman got pregnant. A year later, just like Elisha had promised, she had a son.
The kid grew up. One day, he went out to his dad, who was working with the harvest crew, and started yelling, “My head, my head!”
His dad told a servant, “Carry him to his mother.”
The servant picked him up and brought him to his mom. The boy just lay on her lap until noon, and then he died.
She carried him upstairs and laid him on the bed that belonged to the man of God. She shut the door, leaving him there alone, and then she left.
She called to her husband, “Quick, get me a servant and a donkey. I have to go see the man of God. I’ll be back as fast as I can.”
He asked, “But why today? It’s not a New Moon or Sabbath or anything special.”
She just said, “Don’t ask. I have to go. Now. Trust me.”
She saddled up the donkey and told her servant, “You lead the way, and go as fast as you can. I’ll let you know if you’re going too fast.” And off she went. She found the man of God on Mount Carmel.

The man of God saw her coming from a distance and said to his servant Gehazi, “Look! It’s the Shunammite woman! Run over there and ask her, ‘Is everything okay? Are you good? Is your husband okay? Your kid okay?’”
She just said, “Everything’s fine.”
But when she got to the man of God on the mountain, she fell at his feet and just clung to him.
Gehazi tried to pull her off, but the man of God said, “Leave her alone. Can’t you see she’s in major distress? God hasn’t told me what’s wrong; I’m totally in the dark here.”
Then she finally said it: “Did I even ask you for a son, master? Didn’t I tell you not to mess with me and give me false hope?”
He immediately ordered Gehazi, “No time to waste. Grab my staff and run. Don’t stop to say hi to anyone. If someone says hi to you, just ignore them. Lay my staff on the boy’s face.”
The boy’s mom said, “As sure as God lives and you live, you’re not leaving me behind.” So Gehazi let her go first, and Elisha followed her.
Gehazi got there first and laid the staff on the boy’s face. But there was nothing. No sound, no sign of life. Gehazi went back to meet Elisha and told him, “The boy didn’t even move.”

Elisha went into the house and saw the boy lying dead on the bed. He went into the room, locked the door so it was just the two of them, and prayed to God. Then he got on the bed and lay on top of the boy, covering him with his own body—mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands. As he was stretched out over him, the boy’s body started to get warm. Elisha got up and walked around the room for a bit. Then he went back and stretched out on the boy again. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
He called Gehazi and said, “Get the Shunammite woman in here!” He called her and she came in.
Elisha said, “Go hug your son.”
She fell at Elisha’s feet, face on the ground, totally in awe. Then she hugged her son and walked out with him.
Elisha went back to Gilgal, where there was a huge famine. While he was meeting with the group of prophets, he told his servant, “Put a big pot on the fire and cook some stew for everyone.”

One of the guys went out to a field to find some herbs. He found a wild vine and picked a bunch of gourds from it, filling his bag. He brought them back, chopped them up, and threw them in the stew, even though nobody knew what they were. The stew was served, and the men started to eat. But then they all screamed, “Death in the pot, O man of God! Death in the pot!” No one could eat it.
Elisha said, “Bring me some flour.” He sprinkled it into the pot.
“Okay, serve it to the men now,” he said. They ate it, and it was totally fine—nothing wrong with the stew at all.
Another day, a man came from a place called Baal Shalishah. He brought the man of God twenty loaves of fresh bread from the first harvest, and some fresh grain straight from the first harvest.
Elisha said, “Pass it out for everyone to eat.”
His servant was like, “For a hundred guys? No way, this is not nearly enough!”
Elisha just said, “Do it. God says there’s more than enough.”
And for real, there was. He passed out what he had, and not only did everyone eat, but there were leftovers.

title: This General's Wild Skin Transformation
paragraphs: So, there was this guy Naaman, the top general for the king of Aram. He was a big deal, super respected by his boss because God had used him to win battles for Aram. A total legend, but he had this really bad skin problem. Anyway, during one of their raids on Israel, they captured this young girl who ended up working for Naaman's wife. One day, she told her mistress, "If only my master could meet the prophet of Samaria, he would be healed of his skin disease."
Naaman went straight to his master and told him what the girl from Israel had said.
"Alright, go," said the king of Aram. "I'll even write you a letter to the king of Israel so he knows you're coming."
So Naaman took off with about 750 pounds of silver, 150 pounds of gold, and ten sets of clothes.
Naaman gave the letter to the king of Israel. It was like, "When you get this, know that I'm sending my guy Naaman to you. Heal his skin condition."

When the king of Israel read the letter, he freaked out and ripped his clothes. He was like, "Am I a god? Can I kill people and bring them back to life? Why is he sending this guy to me to be healed? That king's just trying to pick a fight, that's what!"

Elisha, the man of God, heard that the king of Israel was so stressed he ripped his clothes. He sent a message to the king, saying, "Why are you bugging out and ripping your clothes? Send him to me, and he'll find out there's a real prophet in Israel."
So Naaman rolled up with his horses and chariots and pulled up to Elisha's front door.
Elisha didn't even come out. He just sent a servant with a message: "Go wash yourself in the Jordan River seven times. Your skin will be all better, good as new."

Naaman was so mad. He turned around and was like, "I thought he'd at least come out and see me, pray to his God, wave his hand over my skin, and heal me. The rivers in Damascus, the Abana and Pharpar, are way cleaner than any river in Israel. Why can't I just wash in them and get clean?" He stormed off, super ticked.

But his servants ran after him and said, "Father, if the prophet had asked you to do something crazy and heroic, you would've done it, right? So why not just do this simple thing, 'wash and be clean'?"
So he did it. He went down to the Jordan and dipped himself in seven times, just like the man of God said. And his skin was totally healed, smooth like a baby's. He was brand new.

Then he went back to the man of God with his whole crew, stood in front of him, and said, "Okay, now I know for sure that there's no other God on earth but the God of Israel. For real. As a thank you, please take this gift."
"As God lives," Elisha said, "the God I serve, I'm not taking anything from you." Naaman tried to get him to take it, but he wouldn't.

"If you won't take it," Naaman said, "then let me ask for something. Can I get some dirt, like, as much as two donkeys can carry? Because I'm never going to worship any other god but God again. But, uh, there's one thing I need God to forgive me for. When my master leans on my arm and goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship, and I'm there with him, bowing down too, I hope God will forgive me for that."
Elisha said, "It's all good. Go in peace."

But he hadn't gone far when Gehazi, Elisha's servant, thought to himself, "My master just let this Aramean Naaman slip through his fingers without even a thank-you. By the living God, I'm going after him to get something." And Gehazi ran after Naaman.
Naaman saw him running and jumped down from his chariot to meet him. "Is everything okay?"

"Yeah, everything's fine, but something came up. My master sent me to tell you that two young prophets just showed up from the hill country of Ephraim. He said to give them a gift of 75 pounds of silver and a couple of sets of clothes."
Naaman said, "Of course, how about 150 pounds?" He insisted, tied up the money in two bags, gave him the two sets of clothes, and even sent two of his own servants to carry the stuff back for him.
When they got to the hill, Gehazi took the gifts from the servants, hid them inside, and sent the servants away.
He went back and stood before his master. Elisha asked, "So, what were you up to, Gehazi?"
"Nothing much," he said.

Elisha said, "Didn't you know I was with you in spirit when that man got down from his chariot to meet you? Seriously, is this the time to be lining your own pockets with gifts? Naaman's skin disease is now going to be on you and your family, forever." Gehazi walked away, and his skin was all white and flaky, like snow.

title: Floating Axe Heads & Invisible Armies?!
paragraphs: One day, the crew of prophets went to Elisha and were like, "Look, this place we're living in with you is getting seriously cramped. We have no elbow room."
They said, "Can we get permission to go down to the Jordan River? Each of us can grab a log and we'll build a bigger place."
Elisha was fine with it. "Go ahead," he said.
Then one of them was like, "Please! You should totally come with us!"
"For sure," Elisha replied.
So he went with them. They got to the Jordan and started chopping down trees. As one of the guys was cutting down a big piece of timber, his axe head flew right off and sank in the river.
"Oh no, master!" he yelled. "And it was borrowed!"
The Holy Man asked, "Where did it sink?"
The guy showed him the spot.
Elisha cut a branch off a tree and tossed it right where the axe head fell. And you won't believe this—the axe head floated to the surface.
"Go grab it," he said. The man reached out and took it.
Another time, the king of Aram was at war with Israel. He had a meeting with his officers and said, "I want to set up an ambush at this specific spot."
But the Holy Man sent a message to the king of Israel: "Watch out when you pass by this place, because the Arameans have set up a trap there."
So the king of Israel sent a warning to the people at the place the Holy Man had told him about.
This kind of thing happened all the time.
The king of Aram was absolutely furious about this. He got his officers together and demanded, "Tell me, who is leaking information to the king of Israel? Who is the spy in our group?"
But one of his officers said, "It's not us, my king. It's Elisha, the prophet in Israel. He tells the king of Israel literally everything you say, even the stuff you whisper in your bedroom."
The king ordered, "Go find out where he is. I'll send people to capture him."
The report came back: "He's in Dothan."
So the king sent out horses and chariots—a huge, impressive army. They traveled by night and surrounded the city.
Early the next morning, a servant of the Holy Man got up and went outside. Surprise! The city was surrounded by horses and chariots. The young man freaked out, "Oh, master! What are we going to do?"
Elisha told him, "Don't even worry about it. There are more on our side than on their side."
Then Elisha prayed, "O God, open his eyes and let him see."
And God opened the young man's eyes. He looked, and it was a wonder. The entire mountainside was filled with horses and chariots of fire, all surrounding Elisha.
When the Arameans started to attack, Elisha prayed to God, "Strike these people blind!" And God struck them blind, just as Elisha had asked.
Then Elisha called out to the blind army, "You're going the wrong way! This isn't the right city! Follow me, and I'll lead you to the man you're looking for." And he led them all the way to Samaria.
As they entered the city, Elisha prayed, "O God, open their eyes so they can see where they are." God opened their eyes, and they looked around—they were trapped inside Samaria!
When the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha, "Father, should I just massacre them all?"
"Not a chance!" said Elisha. "You didn't do anything to capture them, so why would you kill them? No way. Make a big feast for them and then send them back to their master."
So the king prepared a huge feast for them. After they had eaten and drunk as much as they wanted, he sent them home. After that, the raiding parties from Aram stopped bothering Israel for a while.

But later, King Ben-Hadad of Aram gathered his entire army and attacked Samaria, laying siege to it. This caused a terrible famine, so bad that food prices went through the roof. A donkey's head cost eighty shekels of silver, and a small bowl of field greens cost five shekels!
One day, the king of Israel was walking along the city wall when a woman cried out to him, "Help me, your majesty!"
He answered, "If God won't help you, how can I? Should I get you grain from the granary? Or wine from the winepress?"
The king then said, "Tell me what's wrong."

She said, "This woman came to me and said, 'Give me your son, and we'll eat him today. Tomorrow, we'll eat my son.' So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day, I told her, 'It's your turn—bring your son so we can eat him.' But she had hidden her son away."

When the king heard the woman's story, he tore his robes in grief. Since he was on the city wall, everyone saw that he was wearing coarse burlap under his clothes as a sign of mourning. And he shouted, "May God strike me down if Elisha son of Shaphat still has his head on his shoulders by the end of today!"

Elisha was at home, sitting with the elders. The king had already sent an executioner, but before the man arrived, Elisha said to the elders, "Do you know that this murderer has just sent a man to cut off my head? Look, when the executioner gets here, shut the door and lock it. Don't I hear the footsteps of his master right behind him?"
While he was still talking, the king himself showed up and accused him, saying, "This disaster is from God! What's next? I'm so done with God!"

title: From Starving to Feasting, Like, Overnight
paragraphs: Elisha said, “Listen up! God’s got something to say. The famine is officially over. By this time tomorrow, food will be super cheap and everywhere—a bunch of flour for a single coin, two big scoops of grain for a single coin. The market at the city gate is gonna be popping.”
But the official the king leaned on for support scoffed at the Holy Man: “You expect us to believe that? Like trapdoors are gonna open in the sky and food will just tumble out?”
Elisha shot back, “Oh, you’ll see it happen with your own eyes, but you won’t get to eat a single bite.”

Meanwhile, there were four guys with leprosy just chilling outside the city gate. They said to each other, “Bro, what are we doing just sitting here waiting to die? If we go into the city, we’ll starve to death with everyone else. If we stay here, we’ll die too. So, let's just take a chance and sneak over to the Aramean camp. If they let us live, cool. If they kill us, well, we were gonna die anyway. We’ve got nothing to lose.”

So when the sun went down, they got up and headed to the Aramean camp. But when they got to the edge of it, plot twist! There was literally no one there. Turns out, the Lord had made the whole Aramean army hear what sounded like a massive army with chariots and horses charging at them. They said to one another, “The king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to attack us!” They totally panicked and ran for their lives in the middle of the night, leaving everything behind—tents, horses, donkeys, the whole camp was just left as is. These four lepers entered the camp and went into a tent. First they ate and drank. Then they grabbed a bunch of silver, gold, and clothes, and went and hid it all. They came back, looted another tent, and hid that stuff too.

Finally, they looked at each other and were like, “Okay, we probably shouldn’t be doing this. This is a day of amazing news, and we’re just keeping it to ourselves. That's lowkey selfish. If we wait until morning, we’re gonna get in trouble. Let’s go tell the king’s palace right now.”

So they went back to the city gate and shouted the news, “We went to the Aramean camp and—you’re not gonna believe this—it’s completely empty. Not a single person, not a sound! The horses and donkeys are still tied up, and the tents are just sitting there.”

The gatekeepers passed the message all the way to the king's palace. Roused in the middle of the night, the king told his servants, “I know what’s going on. The Arameans know we’re starving. They’ve left their camp and are hiding in the fields. They’re thinking, ‘When the Israelites come out, we’ll capture them and take over the city.’”

But one of his advisors said, “Hold up, let’s send some guys with five of the remaining horses. I mean, the worst that can happen to them is the same thing that could happen to any of us left in the city. Let’s just send them to see what’s up.”
So they sent out two chariots with horses. The king ordered them, “Go follow the Aramean army and find out what happened.”

They followed the trail all the way to the Jordan River, and the whole path was littered with clothes and gear that the Arameans had ditched in their rush to escape. The scouts came back and told the king everything.

Then the people rushed out and looted the entire Aramean camp. Just like God said, food prices crashed overnight. You could get a bunch of flour for a single coin, and two big scoops of grain for one coin. It was wild.

The king had put his attendant, the one he leaned on for support, in charge of the gate. But the starving people were like a mob and just poured through the gate, trampling the official to death in the chaos. It happened exactly like the prophet had said it would when the king visited him.

Every single thing the prophet told the king came true. He said, “A bunch of flour for a coin, two big scoops of grain for a coin, this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria.” And when the official had replied with a sarcastic, “You expect us to believe that? Like trapdoors are gonna open in the sky and food will just tumble out?” the prophet had said, “You’ll see it with your own eyes, but you won’t eat a single bite.” And that’s exactly what happened. The final detail was the people trampling him to death at the gate.

title: Prophecies, Betrayal, and a Wild Ride for the Throne
paragraphs: Years before, Elisha told this woman whose son he'd brought back to life, "Leave here and go, you and your family, and live someplace else. God has ordered a seven-year famine on this land." The woman did what the prophet told her: she left with her family and lived as aliens in the country of Philistia for seven years. When the seven years were over, they came back and she went straight to the king to get her house and land back.

At that exact moment, the king was chatting with Gehazi, Elisha's assistant, and said, "Bro, tell me some of the wild stuff Elisha has done." And right as Gehazi was telling the king about how Elisha brought a dead person back to life, the *actual* woman whose son was resurrected showed up, asking for her property back. The timing was insane.
Gehazi was like, "My king, no way! This is her! This is the lady, and that's her son who Elisha brought back from the dead!"

The king was shook and wanted the whole story, so she told him everything. Then the king put an official on the case and said, "Make sure she gets all her stuff back, plus all the money her farm made while she was gone."
Later, Elisha went to Damascus. The king of Aram, Ben-Hadad, was super sick. Someone told him, "The Holy Man is in town."
The king ordered Hazael, "Take a gift with you and go meet the Holy Man. Ask God through him if I'm gonna get better from this sickness."

Hazael went to meet Elisha with a ton of gifts from Damascus—like, 40 camel-loads of the best stuff! He stood in front of Elisha and said, "Your son, King Ben-Hadad of Aram, sent me to ask you: 'Am I going to recover from this sickness?'"

Elisha answered, "Go tell him, 'Don't worry, you'll live.' But the fact is, God showed me that he's doomed to die." Then Elisha stared hard at Hazael, reading his heart. Hazael felt exposed and dropped his eyes. Then the prophet started crying.
Hazael asked, "My lord, why are you crying?"

Elisha said, "Because I know the terrible things you're going to do to the people of Israel. You're gonna burn down their fortresses, murder their young men, smash their babies, and rip open their pregnant women."
Hazael said, "Am I a mongrel dog that I'd do such a horrible thing?"
Elisha just said, "God showed me that you will be the king of Aram."
Hazael left and went back to his king, who asked, "So, what did Elisha say?"
He said, "He told me, 'Don't worry, you'll live.'"
But the very next day, someone took a thick blanket, soaked it in water, and held it over the king's face until he suffocated. And just like that, Hazael became king.

In the fifth year that Joram, son of Ahab, was king of Israel, Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, became king of Judah. He was 32 when he started his reign, and he was king in Jerusalem for eight years. He totally copied the lifestyle of the kings of Israel, even marrying into Ahab's messed-up family. From God's POV, he was just another evil dude living an evil life. But because of his promise to David, God wasn't ready to destroy Judah yet. He had promised to keep a light shining for David's descendants.
During Jehoram's rule, Edom rebelled against Judah and got their own king. Jehoram took his army and chariots to a place called Zair to deal with it.
The Edomites surrounded him, but in the middle of the night, he and his chariot commanders broke through their lines and wrecked them. But then his own soldiers bailed on him.
Edom is still in rebellion against Judah to this day. Even the small town of Libnah rebelled at that time.

The rest of the story of Jehoram's life and his rule is written in *The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah*. Jehoram died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Ahaziah took over as king.

In the twelfth year that Joram, son of Ahab, was king of Israel, Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, became king of Judah. Ahaziah was 22 when he started his reign, and he only ruled for a year in Jerusalem. His mom was Athaliah, the granddaughter of King Omri of Israel. He lived and ruled just like the Ahab family, continuing their legacy of doing evil in God's eyes. He was connected to the Ahab family by marriage and by sin.

He teamed up with Joram, son of Ahab, to fight against King Hazael of Aram at Ramoth Gilead. Joram got wounded by archers and had to go back to Jezreel to recover. Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went to visit Joram while he was on his sickbed in Jezreel.

title: Jehu's Takeover
paragraphs: So, one day, Elisha the prophet gave a clear order to one of the younger prophets, a guy from the prophet-in-training squad. "Alright, listen up," Elisha said. "Get yourself ready, grab a flask of olive oil, and head straight to Ramoth Gilead. Your mission is to find this guy named Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. Once you spot him, pull him aside from his buddies and take him somewhere private, like a back room. Then, pour that oil over his head and tell him, 'This is God's message: I'm anointing you as king over Israel!' After that, open the door and bolt out of there as fast as your legs can carry you. Seriously, don't even stick around for a second!"

The young prophet did exactly what he was told and headed to Ramoth Gilead. When he got there, he found all the army officers just chilling, sitting around together. He walked up and said, "Hey, officer, I've got something important I need to talk to you about." Jehu, probably looking around at the other guys, asked, "Uh, which one of us are you talking to?" The prophet pointed directly at him and said, "No, I mean *you*, officer."

Jehu got up and followed the young prophet inside the building. The prophet poured the oil on Jehu's head and declared, "This is God's word, from the God of Israel: I've just anointed you to be king over God's people, over Israel! Your first big assignment is to totally take down the government of Ahab, your master. I'm getting payback for the brutal murders of my servants, the prophets—yeah, I'm talking about that massacre Jezebel orchestrated against all of God's prophets.

The whole family line of Ahab is toast! I'm wiping out every single one of those pathetic people. I'm going to make sure that Ahab's family ends up just like the family of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, and the family of Baasha, son of Ahijah. And as for Jezebel? The dogs are going to eat her dead body right out in the open fields of Jezreel. She won't even get a proper burial!" Then, without another word, he opened the door and ran for it.
Jehu walked back out to his master's officers. They immediately asked him, "Is everything cool? What did that crazy weirdo want with you?"
Jehu played it cool, saying, "Oh, you know how those kinds of guys are—all talk, nothing serious."
"That's a lie!" they snapped back. "Spill it! What happened?" Jehu finally gave in and said, "Okay, fine. He told me this, this, and this—basically, 'God's word: I'm anointing you king of Israel!'"

Suddenly, they were all hyped up! Each man quickly grabbed his cloak and piled them up at the top of the steps to make a makeshift throne for Jehu. Then, they blasted the trumpet and shouted, "Jehu is king!"

And just like that, the whole plot by Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi, against King Joram was officially in motion. Meanwhile, Joram and his whole army were busy defending Ramoth Gilead from Hazael, the king of Aram (Syria).

But Joram had actually pulled back to Jezreel to recover from the injuries he got battling the Arameans and their king, Hazael. Jehu, now feeling like a king, told his officers, "If you guys are serious about me being king, then don't let anyone sneak out of this city and blab the news back in Jezreel!"
Then Jehu hopped into a chariot and rode straight to Jezreel, where King Joram was chilling in bed, recuperating. King Ahaziah of Judah had also come down to visit Joram.

A guard standing watch on the tower in Jezreel spotted Jehu's group arriving. He called out, "Hey, I see a bunch of men coming!" Joram said, "Send a horseman out to meet them and ask, 'Is everything alright? Is it peaceful?'"

The horseman rode out to meet Jehu and asked, "The king wants to know if everything's okay." Jehu shot back, "What does it matter to you whether things are okay or not? Just fall in behind me!" The sentry on the tower reported, "The messenger reached them, but he's not coming back."

The king then sent out a second horseman. When he reached Jehu's group, he asked, "The king wants to know if everything's okay." Jehu gave him the same answer: "What does it matter to you whether things are okay or not? Just fall in behind me!"
The sentry on the tower called out again, "The second messenger reached them, but he's not coming back either! And the way they're driving—it's just like the crazy driving of Jehu, son of Nimshi!"

Joram immediately ordered, "Get my chariot ready!" So, they hitched up his chariot. King Joram of Israel and King Ahaziah of Judah, each in his own chariot, drove out to meet Jehu. They met up in the field that used to belong to Naboth in Jezreel.

When Joram saw Jehu, he called out, "Is everything good, Jehu?" Jehu shot back, "What's good about it? How can anything be good as long as your mother Jezebel's disgusting promiscuity and sorceries are polluting the whole country?"
Joram quickly spun his chariot around and tried to flee, yelling to Ahaziah, "It's a trap, Ahaziah!"
Jehu pulled back his bow and let an arrow fly. It hit Joram right between his shoulder blades and went straight through his heart. He slumped down to his knees in his chariot.

Jehu then ordered Bidkar, his second-in-command, "Quick—throw him into the field of Naboth of Jezreel! Remember when you and I were driving our chariots right behind his father Ahab? That's when God declared this judgment on him: 'As sure as I saw the blood of Naboth and his sons murdered yesterday, you'll pay for it right here on this exact piece of ground. That's God's word!' So, go ahead and throw him out in the field. God's instructions carried out exactly!"

King Ahaziah of Judah saw what was happening and made a run for it, heading down the road toward Beth Haggan. Jehu chased after him, yelling, "Get him, too!" Jehu's troops shot and wounded Ahaziah in his chariot on the hill leading up to Gur, near Ibleam. He managed to make it as far as Megiddo, but that's where he died.
His assistants drove him on to Jerusalem, where they buried him in the family burial plot in the City of David.
It's worth noting that Ahaziah had become king of Judah in the eleventh year of Joram, son of Ahab's reign.

When Jezebel heard that Jehu had arrived in Jezreel, she totally made herself up—she put on eyeshadow, styled her hair, and then posed seductively at a window. When Jehu rode through the city gate, she called down to him, "So, how are things, 'Zimri,' you dashing king-killer?" (She was comparing him to Zimri, a previous king who had assassinated his predecessor and reigned for only seven days).
Jehu looked up at the window and shouted, "Is there anyone up there on my side?" Two or three palace eunuchs (male servants) looked out.
He ordered them, "Throw her down!" So, they threw her out the window. Her blood splattered all over the wall and the horses, and Jehu rode over her with his horse's hooves.
Then Jehu went inside and had his lunch. During his meal, he gave orders, "Go take care of that cursed woman; give her a decent burial—after all, she was a king's daughter."

They went out to bury her, but by then, there was nothing left of her except her skull, feet, and hands. They came back and told Jehu. He said, "This is God's word, the word spoken by Elijah the Tishbite:
"'In the field of Jezreel, dogs will eat Jezebel;
The body of Jezebel will be like dog-droppings on the ground in Jezreel. Old friends and lovers will say, 'I wonder, is this Jezebel?'"

title: Jehu's Purge Goes Viral
paragraphs: So, Ahab had seventy sons still hanging out in Samaria. Jehu shot off some letters to the big shots in Jezreel—the city elders and the guys looking after Ahab’s sons. He basically wrote:

This is your heads-up. You've got your master's kids, all the chariots, horses, a fortified city, and weapons. So pick the best and most qualified of your master's sons, put him on the throne, and get ready to fight for your old boss's dynasty.
They were totally shook by the letter. They were like, “Dude, he already took out two kings. What chance do we have?”

So, the palace manager, the mayor, the elders, and the guardians all sent a message back to Jehu saying, “We’re your servants now. We'll do whatever you say. We're not picking a new king. You're the boss—do what you think is best.”
Then Jehu sent a second letter:
If you're really on my team and ready to follow orders, here's the deal: decapitate your master's sons and bring their heads to me in Jezreel by this time tomorrow.

The king's sons, all seventy of them, were being raised by the city's leaders. When they got that letter, they grabbed all seventy sons and killed them. Then they put their heads in baskets and shipped them off to Jehu in Jezreel.
A messenger came to Jehu and said, “They’ve delivered the heads of the king’s sons.”
He said, “Stack them in two piles at the city gate and leave them there till morning.”

In the morning, Jehu went out, stood in front of everyone, and gave a speech: “You guys are actually part of God’s righteous plan today. Yeah, I'm the one who conspired against my master and killed him. But who do you think is responsible for this pile of heads? Know this for sure: not a single word God spoke against Ahab's family has been canceled. You're seeing it happen right now—God doing exactly what he said he'd do through Elijah.”
Then Jehu went on a spree and killed everyone even remotely connected to Ahab's family in Jezreel—leaders, friends, priests. He wiped them all out.
After that, he dusted himself off and headed to Samaria. On the way, at a place called Beth Eked of the Shepherds, he ran into some relatives of King Ahaziah of Judah.
Jehu asked, “Who are you?”
They said, “We’re Ahaziah’s relatives, and we're heading down for a royal family reunion.”
“Grab them!” Jehu ordered. His men captured them and then slaughtered all forty-two of them at the well of Beth Eked. There were no survivors.
He kept going and then ran into Jehonadab the Recabite, who was on his way to meet him. Jehu greeted him and said, “Are we on the same page here? Are you with me on this?”
Jehonadab said, “Totally. You can count on me.”
“Then give me your hand,” said Jehu.
They shook on it, and Jehonadab hopped into the chariot with Jehu.
“Come with me,” Jehu said, “and see how passionate I am for God.” So they rode off together in the chariot.
When they got to Samaria, Jehu killed everyone left in the city who had any connection to Ahab. It was a total wipeout, just like God had told Elijah would happen.
Next, Jehu gathered all the people and made an announcement:
Ahab was a part-time Baal worshiper; I'm going to be a full-time, hardcore one.

“Get all the prophets of Baal here—every single servant and priest. Don't leave anyone out. I’m about to throw a huge sacrifice for Baal. If you don't show up, you're dead.” (This was a total lie, of course. Jehu was planning to destroy all of Baal's worshipers.)
Jehu ordered, “Set up a special holy event for Baal.” So they did, and they announced the date.
Jehu then sent word to everyone in Israel. They all came—every single Baal worshiper in the country. No one stayed home. They flooded into Baal's temple until it was packed.
Jehu told the guy in charge of the wardrobe, “Get robes for all the servants of Baal.” And he brought them out.

Then Jehu and Jehonadab the Recabite went into the temple of Baal and said, “Double-check and make sure there are no worshipers of God in here. Only Baal worshipers allowed.” Then they started the worship service with sacrifices and burnt offerings.
Meanwhile, Jehu had eighty of his men waiting outside with these orders: “Don’t let a single person escape. If you do, you'll pay with your own life.”
As soon as Jehu finished the sacrificial ceremony, he gave the signal to his officers and guards: “Go in and kill them all! No survivors!”

And the massacre began. The officers and guards threw the bodies outside and cleared a path to the inner shrine of Baal. They dragged out the sacred stone pillar from Baal's temple and smashed it to pieces. They destroyed the Baal altars and tore down the temple. It’s been a public toilet ever since.
And that’s the story of how Jehu got rid of Baal worship in Israel.

But even after all that, Jehu didn't stop committing the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, the sins that had dragged Israel into a sinful lifestyle—the golden calves in Bethel and Dan were left untouched.
God told Jehu, “You did a good job doing what I wanted. You followed my orders against Ahab's family. As a reward, your sons will sit on the throne of Israel for four generations.”
Even so, Jehu wasn't careful to follow God's ways with his whole heart. He didn't turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into a life of sin.

It was around this time that God started to shrink Israel's territory. Hazael started chipping away at the borders of Israel east of the Jordan—all the land of Gilead, Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh, from Aroer near the Arnon Gorge. Basically, all of Gilead and Bashan.

The rest of Jehu's life story, all his accomplishments and his fame, are written in The Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. Jehu died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz became the next king. Jehu ruled Israel from Samaria for twenty-eight years.

title: The Hidden King's Epic Comeback
paragraphs: So, Ahaziah's mom, Athaliah, found out her son was dead and went full-on power hungry. She decided to wipe out the entire royal family to secure her spot on the throne. But plot twist! Jehosheba, who was King Jehoram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, snatched Ahaziah's baby son, Joash, right before he was about to get axed with the other princes. She stashed him and his nanny in a secret room, totally off Athaliah's radar. He survived, and they stayed hidden in God's Temple for six whole years. Meanwhile, Athaliah was running the country, completely clueless that the real heir was still alive.

In the seventh year, this priest named Jehoiada calls a secret meeting with the top security guys—the captains of the bodyguards and the palace guards. They all meet up at The Temple of God. He makes them swear a super serious oath of secrecy, and then, boom, he reveals the hidden prince, Joash.

Then he lays down the plan: 'Alright, listen up. All of you—the guys starting your Sabbath shift at the palace and the guys finishing up your Sabbath shift at The Temple of God—you're gonna team up during the guard change. Form a human shield around the new king, and be ready to fight. If anyone even *tries* to get through, take them out. Your one and only job is to protect the king, 24/7, wherever he goes.'

The captains were all in. They gathered their squads—both the guys starting their Sabbath shift and the guys finishing up their Sabbath shift—and reported to Jehoiada. The priest then hooks them up with some legendary gear: spears and shields that used to belong to King David himself, which had been kept in The Temple of God. Now fully kitted out, the guards got into position, from one end of The Temple to the other, making a protective circle around the Altar and the Temple, ready to defend the king.

The priest then brought out the prince, put the crown on his head, gave him the official scroll of God's laws, and officially made him king. They anointed him with oil, and everyone just went wild, cheering and shouting, 'Long live the king!'

Athaliah heard all the noise from the guards and the crowd and rushed over to The Temple of God to see what was up. She was shook. There was the new king, standing by the royal throne, surrounded by his captains and trumpeters, and the whole crowd was celebrating like crazy with trumpets blasting. Athaliah freaked out, tore her clothes, and started screaming, 'Treason! Treason!'

Jehoiada the priest ordered the army officers, 'Get her out of here! And if anyone tries to help her, kill them on the spot!' He had already told them not to kill her inside The Temple of God. So they grabbed her and dragged her out to the palace's horse entrance, and that's where they finished her.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant, a solemn promise, between God, the king, and the people, that they would be God's people. He also made a pact between the king and the people.
The people then stormed the temple of Baal and completely wrecked it. They smashed the altars and idols into a million pieces and killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, right in front of his own altar.

Jehoiada then set up guards for God's Temple. He had the bodyguard officers, the palace security, and all the people escort the king from the Temple, through the main Guard's Gate, and into the royal palace. There, he sat on the king's throne. The whole city celebrated, and everything was finally chill and peaceful. And as for Athaliah, she was taken care of with the royal sword.
Joash was only seven years old when he became king.

title: Temple Flip Turns Deadly
paragraphs: So, in Jehu's seventh year as king, this dude Joash steps up and starts his own reign. He was king in Jerusalem for a solid 40 years. His mom was a woman named Zibiah from Beersheba.

Basically, for as long as the priest Jehoiada was teaching and training him, Joash did what was right in God's eyes. (But, lowkey, he never got around to tearing down the sketchy hilltop shrines—people were still going there all the time, making sacrifices and burning incense.)

Joash told the priests, "All the money that comes into God's Temple for offerings—whether it's the required stuff or people just giving it freely—let's use it to fix up the Temple wherever it's falling apart. Just make sure you keep track of it all."
But fast-forward 23 years into Joash's rule, and the priests hadn't done a single thing. The Temple was still a total wreck.

So King Joash calls in Jehoiada the priest and his whole crew and is like, "Uh, why haven't you renovated this beat-up Temple? You're cut off. No more taking money for Temple repairs. From now on, hand over every single coin you get."
The priests had to agree to stop taking the money and to stay out of the renovation project.

Then Jehoiada got this idea. He took a chest, cut a hole in the lid, and put it right by the main entrance of God's Temple. All the offerings people brought were dropped into that chest by the priests guarding the door. Whenever they saw the chest was getting full, the king's secretary and the head priest would come, empty it out, and count all the money. They'd give the counted cash to the project managers, who then paid the carpenters, builders, masons, and stonecutters. They also used it to buy timber and stone for the repairs—basically, any expense for fixing up God's Temple. But none of that money was used for the fancy extras, like silver cups, candle snuffers, or gold and silver instruments. It all went to the workers fixing the Temple. And get this—they trusted the guys handling the money so much that they didn't even need to audit them. They were just straight-up honest dudes. The only money that didn't go into the building fund was from the special offerings for guilt and sin—that money went directly to the priests.

Around this time, King Hazael of Aram went and attacked Gath, and he actually captured it. Then he got ambitious and set his sights on Jerusalem. Joash, the king of Judah, countered by gathering up all the sacred stuff his ancestors—kings Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah—had dedicated, plus his own holy gifts. He also grabbed all the gold he could find in the temple and palace storerooms and sent it all as a massive bribe to King Hazael. That did the trick. Appeased, Hazael went on his way and didn't bother Jerusalem.

The rest of the story of Joash, and everything he did, is all written down in the official records of the kings of Judah. But it ends pretty badly for him. His own palace staff plotted against him and assassinated him while he was taking a walk on the ramp of the city's outer wall. The assassins were Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer. And that's how Joash died. He was buried in the royal tombs in the City of David, and his son Amaziah became the next king.

title: Elisha's Last Prophecy & a Dude Comes Back to Life?!
paragraphs: Alright, so in the 23rd year that Joash son of Ahaziah was king of Judah, this dude Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, became the king of Israel in Samaria. He was in charge for seventeen years, and honestly, he was kinda trash. He was doing all sorts of evil stuff in God's eyes, basically just copying the terrible example of Jeroboam son of Nebat, the guy who got Israel into sin in the first place. He didn't even try to be better. Exasperated, God was furious with Israel, so He let King Hazael of Aram and his son Ben-Hadad just walk all over them. This went on for a super long time.

Then Jehoahaz finally prayed for God to ease up on his anger, and God actually listened. He saw how messed up life was for the Israelites because of the king of Aram's cruelty. So God sent a savior for Israel who got them out from under Aram's thumb. The Israelites could finally live in peace in their own homes again. But it was lowkey pointless: they didn't change their lives at all, didn't stop the whole Jeroboam-sin lifestyle that was basically Israel's brand at this point. Plus, those weird sex-and-religion Asherah shrines were still going strong in Samaria.

After Hazael was done with them, Jehoahaz's army was basically non-existent. All he had left were fifty cavalry, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers. The king of Aram had totally wrecked the rest, leaving pretty much nothing.

The rest of the story of Jehoahaz, all the stuff he did, it's all written down in *The Chronicles of the Kings of Israel*. Jehoahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Jehoash took over as king.

In the thirty-seventh year of King Joash of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel in Samaria, and he reigned for sixteen years. In God's eyes, he was also living an evil life. He didn't change a single thing from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel down the path of sin. He just kept on the same track, step by step.

The rest of the story of Jehoash, all his accomplishments and his war against King Amaziah of Judah, are written in *The Chronicles of the Kings of Israel*. Jehoash died and was with his ancestors. Jeroboam took his throne. Jehoash was buried in Samaria in the royal cemetery.

Elisha got super sick, and it was the sickness that he would end up dying from. King Jehoash of Israel went to visit him. When he saw Elisha, he just broke down and cried, saying, “My father, my father! The chariot and horsemen of Israel!”
Elisha told him, “Go get a bow and some arrows.” The king brought him the bow and arrows.
Then he told the king, “Put your hand on the bow.” He put his hand on it. Then Elisha put his own hand over the king's hand.
Elisha said, “Now open the east window.” He opened it.
Then he said, “Shoot!” And he shot.
“That's the arrow of God’s salvation!” Elisha exclaimed. “The arrow of deliverance from Aram! You're gonna fight Aram until there's nothing left of them.”
“Now pick up the other arrows,” said Elisha. He picked them up.
Then he said to the king of Israel, “Strike the ground.”
The king hit the ground three times and then just stopped.
The holy man got angry with him: “Why didn't you hit the ground five or six times? Then you would've beaten Aram until they were completely done for. Now, you'll only defeat them three times.”
Then Elisha died and they buried him.

Some time later, some raiding bands of Moabites, like they usually did, invaded the country. One day, some guys were burying a man and they saw the raiders. They just chucked the body into Elisha’s tomb and ran for it. When the dead guy's body touched Elisha’s bones, the man came back to life, stood up, and just walked out on his own two feet. Wild.

Hazael king of Aram was a total pain and made life miserable for Israel during Jehoahaz's entire reign. But God was gracious and showed them mercy. He stuck with them because of His promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He never gave up on them, never even thought about ditching them, even to this day. Hazael king of Aram died. His son Ben-Hadad became the next king.

Jehoash son of Jehoahaz turned things around and took back the cities that Ben-Hadad son of Hazael had captured from his father Jehoahaz. Jehoash went to war three times and won each time, taking back the cities of Israel.

title: Kings Throwing Shade & Taking L's
paragraphs: Alright, so check it. In the second year of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, this dude Amaziah, son of Joash, took the throne in Judah. He was 25 when he started and ruled for 29 years in Jerusalem. His mom's name was Jehoaddin, and she was a Jerusalem local.

He was, like, mostly a good king who followed God. But he wasn't on the same level as his ancestor David. He was more like his own dad, Joash, and let all those sketchy local shrines stay open, where people were doing all sorts of wild stuff.

Once he had the kingdom on lock, he had the guards who assassinated his father executed. But he didn't kill their sons, which was actually pretty cool of him. He was following God's command written in the Word revealed to Moses: parents don't pay for their kids' sins, and kids don't pay for their parents'. You're responsible for your own mess, you know?
Amaziah had this massive victory against Edom in the Valley of Salt, like, 10,000 casualties. He also conquered a city called The Rock and renamed it Joktheel, which is what it's still called.
But then Amaziah got a big head and challenged Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, king of Israel, to a fight. He said, "Come at me. Let's settle this face-to-face."

Jehoash's reply to Amaziah was savage. He basically told him a story about a little thistle in Lebanon that sent word to a giant cedar in Lebanon, 'Give your daughter to my son in marriage.' But then a wild animal of Lebanon just stepped on it and crushed it. He was saying, "Dude, just because you beat Edom, you think you're a big deal? Be proud, but stay in your lane. Why risk getting wrecked and taking Judah down with you?"
But Amaziah wouldn't listen. So, Jehoash, the king of Israel, went to battle against him at Beth Shemesh in Judah.
And, yeah, Judah got completely owned by Israel. All their soldiers just ran home.

Jehoash of Israel captured Amaziah of Judah, the son of Joash, the son of Ahaziah, at Beth Shemesh. But he didn't stop. He went on to Jerusalem and tore down a huge chunk of the city wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—like 600 feet of it. He looted everything valuable from The Temple of God and the palace—gold, silver, all of it. He even took hostages before heading back to Samaria.

The rest of the story about Jehoash, all his accomplishments, and the beef with Amaziah, is written down in the official records of Israel's kings. Then he died and was buried in Samaria with the other kings, and his son Jeroboam took over.
Amaziah son of Joash, the king of Judah, actually outlived Jehoash son of Jehoahaz of Israel by 15 years. The rest of his life is in the history books of Judah's kings.

Eventually, some people in Jerusalem plotted against Amaziah, and he had to run to a town called Lachish. But they hunted him down and killed him there. They brought his body back on a horse and buried him in Jerusalem with his ancestors.
Then the people of Judah made Amaziah's son, Azariah, the new king. He was only 16! After his dad died, he rebuilt and restored the town of Elath to Judah.

Meanwhile, back in the 15th year of Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Jehoash became the king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for 41 years. And honestly? He was a pretty bad king in God's eyes. He just kept doing all the same sinful stuff that Jeroboam son of Nebat did, leading Israel down the wrong path. But, he did manage to get back some of Israel's old territory, from Lebo Hamath all the way to the Dead Sea. This was actually what God, the God of Israel, had promised through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath Hepher.

See, God knew how much Israel was struggling. Times were tough for everyone—slave or citizen—and there was no help in sight. But God wasn't ready to just erase Israel from the map. So he used Jeroboam son of Jehoash, even though he was a bad king, to save them.

The rest of Jeroboam's story, his wins in battle, and how he got back Damascus and Hamath for Israel, that's all in the history books too. Then Jeroboam died and was buried, and his son Zechariah became the next king.

title: Israel's Royal Rumble: Kings Keep Getting Axed
paragraphs: So in the 27th year that Jeroboam was king of Israel, this guy Azariah, son of Amaziah, became king in Judah. He was only 16 when he started and ended up ruling for a wild 52 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Jecoliah from Jerusalem. He was actually pretty decent in God's eyes, kinda following his dad Amaziah's lead. But, plot twist, he didn't tear down the local shrines where people were doing all sorts of sketchy religious stuff; those places stayed super popular.

Then God hit the king with a nasty skin disease that stuck with him until he died. He had to live in a separate house and couldn't really be king anymore. His son Jotham stepped up to run the government and rule the country for him.

The rest of the story of Azariah, all the stuff he did, is written down in the official records of the kings of Judah. Azariah eventually died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Jotham took over as king.

In the 38th year of Azariah's rule in Judah, Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, became king over Israel in Samaria. But dude only lasted for six months. He was a total mess in God's eyes, just like his ancestors. He kept up the same messed-up traditions of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who got Israel hooked on sin in the first place.
Then this guy Shallum son of Jabesh plotted against him and straight-up assassinated him in front of everyone. Shallum then took over as king.

The rest of Zechariah's short and messy life is all written down in the official records of the kings of Israel. This was basically God's word coming true, the one he gave to Jehu saying, "Your family will rule Israel for four generations." Zechariah was the fourth one. The end.
Shallum son of Jabesh became king in the 39th year of King Azariah of Judah. He was king in Samaria for... wait for it... just one month.
Then Menahem son of Gadi rolled up from Tirzah to Samaria, attacked Shallum son of Jabesh, and killed him. Then he made himself king.
The rest of Shallum's one-month-reign and the whole conspiracy story are written in the official records of the kings of Israel.

Menahem, now king, started his reign from Tirzah by absolutely wrecking the town of Tiphsah and its suburbs just because they didn't welcome him. It got super dark—he brutally killed all the pregnant women there.

In the 39th year of King Azariah of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king over Israel. He ruled from Samaria for ten years. And yeah, he was another evil one in God's book. He just copied all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who got Israel into that whole sin lifestyle.

Then the king of Assyria, Tiglath-Pileser III, showed up and invaded. But Menahem cut a deal with him. He basically bought the Assyrian king's support by giving him 37 tons of silver. He got the cash by taxing every rich landowner in Israel 50 shekels each for the Assyrian king. That made the king of Assyria happy, and he bounced.
The rest of Menahem's life and all his deeds are in the official records of the kings of Israel. Menahem died and was buried, and his son Pekahiah became the next king.

In the 50th year of King Azariah of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for two years. And you guessed it—he was evil in God's eyes. He stayed on the same old sinful path of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel down the wrong road.

But then his own military aide, Pekah son of Remaliah, conspired against him. He straight-up murdered him in his own private room in the palace in Samaria. He also killed two other guys, Argob and Arieh. Fifty Gadites were in on the plot with him. After the murder, Pekah became the new king.
The rest of Pekahiah's life and everything he did is written in the official records of the kings of Israel.

In the 52nd year of King Azariah of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for twenty years. From God's perspective, he was a bad dude. He didn't change a single thing from the sinful path that Jeroboam son of Nebat had started, the one that got Israel sinning.

During Pekah's reign, the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III invaded again. He captured a bunch of towns—Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, basically the whole region of Naphtali—and deported everyone to Assyria.
But then Hoshea son of Elah started a conspiracy against Pekah son of Remaliah. He assassinated him and took over as king. This all happened in the 20th year of Jotham, son of Uzziah's, reign.
The rest of Pekah's story and everything he did is written in the official records of the kings of Israel.

In the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah became king of Judah. He was 25 when he started and ruled for 16 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. He was actually a good king in God's eyes, following his dad Uzziah's example. But he also didn't get rid of the local shrines, and they stayed as popular as ever. He was the one who had the High Gate of God's Temple built.

The rest of Jotham's life and all his accomplishments are written in the official records of the kings of Judah. It was during his time that God started sending Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah to attack Judah. Jotham eventually died and was buried in his family's tomb in the City of David. His son Ahaz became the next king.

title: King Ahaz's Epic Fail & His Knock-Off Altar
paragraphs: So, in the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Ahaz son of Jotham became the king of Judah. He was twenty when he started his reign, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. But get this—he wasn't living right in God's eyes; he was nothing like his ancestor David. He basically copied the playbook of the kings of Israel and even did some seriously messed-up stuff, like sacrificing his own son in a fire ritual. Total pagan move he picked up from the nations God had kicked out of the land earlier. He was also all about those sketchy local shrines for sex and religion that were popping up everywhere.
Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, teamed up to attack Jerusalem. They put the city under siege, but they couldn't actually break through and get to Ahaz.
Around the same time, on another front, the king of Edom took back the port of Elath and kicked out the people of Judah. The Edomites moved in and have been there ever since.

Ahaz was freaking out, so he sent a message to King Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria, saying, "I'm your servant and your son. You gotta come save me from the king of Aram and the king of Israel. They're crushing me right now." Then Ahaz totally looted the treasuries of the palace and God's Temple, grabbing all the gold and silver to send to the Assyrian king as a bribe.
The king of Assyria agreed to help. He went and attacked Damascus, captured it, and deported all the people to Nineveh as exiles. And as for King Rezin? He had him killed.

Later, King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet up with Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria. While he was there, he was super impressed by this altar. He sent a sketch and a full set of blueprints for it back to Uriah the priest. So, Uriah the priest built an identical altar based on the plans Ahaz sent. By the time the king got back from Damascus, the new altar was ready.

The second the king saw the new altar, he went up to it and started a whole worship service. He did all the offerings: Whole-Burnt-Offerings with tons of smoke, Grain-Offerings, Drink-Offerings, and even sprinkled blood from the Peace-Offerings—the whole nine yards. But the original bronze Altar, the one that represented God's presence, he just shoved it aside to make room for his new, fancy one.

Then King Ahaz told Uriah the priest, "From now on, do all the sacrifices on this new, great altar. The morning burnt offerings, the evening grain offerings, the king's offerings, the people's offerings, all of it. Splash all the blood against this altar. The old bronze one? I'll just use that for my own personal stuff."
And Uriah the priest did exactly what King Ahaz told him to do.

Then King Ahaz went on a spree, stripping all the bronze from the Temple's furniture. He even took the four bronze oxen that held up the giant basin, called The Sea, and just plopped The Sea on the stone floor. To top it off, he got rid of any special features in the Temple that he thought might offend the king of Assyria.

For the rest of the story of Ahaz and everything he did, it's all written down in The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Ahaz eventually died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah took over as the next king.

title: Israel Gets DEPORTED?! The OG Cancel Culture
paragraphs: So, in the 12th year that Ahaz was king of Judah, this dude Hoshea, son of Elah, became the king of Israel. He ruled from Samaria for nine years. And from God's POV, he was living a pretty bad life, but honestly, not as bad as the kings that came before him.

Then, Shalmaneser, the king of Assyria, rolled up and attacked. Hoshea was basically already his puppet and had to send him money regularly. But Shalmaneser found out Hoshea was being a total snake behind his back, trying to make a deal with King So of Egypt. And to make it worse, Hoshea was super late on his payments to Assyria. So, the Assyrian king had him arrested and thrown in jail. After that, he just invaded the whole country. He went after Samaria and laid siege to it for three whole years.

In the ninth year of Hoshea's rule, the king of Assyria finally took over Samaria and kicked the Israelites out, sending them into exile in Assyria. He moved them to Halah, to Gozan on the Habor River, and to the towns of the Medes.

This whole exile thing happened because of sin. The people of Israel sinned against their God, the same God who saved them from Egypt and the tyranny of the Pharaoh. They started worshipping other gods, copying the lifestyles of the pagan nations God had already kicked out, and just went along with whatever their own kings wanted. They were doing all sorts of shady stuff against their God, and then they weren't even hiding it anymore, building these gross sex-and-religion shrines all over the place. They put up their weird symbols at basically every corner. Everywhere you looked, they were making offerings to fake gods—the same exact stuff that got the other nations exiled in the first place. They racked up a huge list of evil deeds, and God was just completely over it, especially their obsession with worshipping idols made of wood and clay, even though He had clearly told them, "Don't do this—ever!"

God had warned Israel and Judah, sending a ton of prophets and seers over and over again to tell them, "Turn away from your evil lifestyle. Just do what I say, follow the rules I gave your ancestors and have been reminding you about through my prophets."

But they just wouldn't listen. If anything, they were even more stubborn than their ancestors, which is saying something. They totally disrespected His instructions, the sacred promise He made with their ancestors, and all His warnings. They started living for nothing and basically became nothing, just like the pagan people around them. God had given them a clear warning: "Don't do it!" but they did it anyway.

They tossed out everything their God had told them. They replaced Him with two statues of bull-calves and a pole for some goddess named Asherah. They started worshipping stars and planets and were always at the sex-and-religion shrines for Baal. They even stooped so low as to sacrifice their own sons and daughters as burnt offerings! They got into all kinds of dark magic and sorcery. Basically, they sold themselves out to every evil thing they could find. And God had finally had enough.

God was so incredibly angry that He just got rid of them, kicked them out of the country for good, until only the tribe of Judah was left. (And honestly, Judah wasn't much better. They didn't follow God's commands either and fell into the same bad habits as Israel.) God rejected everyone connected to Israel, made their lives super hard, and let anyone who wanted to take advantage of them do it. And then came the final "No" as He threw them out of His sight.

This all goes back to when God ripped Israel away from David's family line, and they made Jeroboam son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam totally corrupted Israel—he turned them away from God and led them into a life full of sin. The Israelites just went along with all the sins Jeroboam introduced; they never even complained. In the end, God had to say a final "No" to Israel and turn His back on them. He had given them plenty of fair warnings through His prophets. Then He exiled Israel from their own land to Assyria. And that's where they still are today.

The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and moved them into the towns of Samaria to replace the exiled Israelites. They just moved in and took over like they owned the place. When the Assyrians first moved in, they treated God like just another random god; they didn't respect or worship Him. So, God sent lions that started attacking and killing them.

A message was sent back to the king of Assyria: "Hey, the people you sent to live in Samaria don't know the rules of the local god, and now he's sending lions to kill them because nobody knows what he wants."
So the king of Assyria commanded, "Send back one of the priests we exiled from there. Let him go back and live there and teach the people what the god of the land expects."
So one of the priests who had been exiled from Samaria came back and settled in Bethel. He started teaching them how to properly worship God.

But every group of people that Assyria had settled there just went ahead and made their own gods anyway. They set them up in the local shrines that the people of Samaria had left behind. It was like a custom-made god for each town.

For Babylon, it was Succoth Benoth; for Cuthah, it was Nergal; for Hamath, Ashima; for Avva, Nibhaz and Tartak; for Sepharvaim, Adrammelech and Anammelech (they would even burn their own children as sacrifices to these gods!).

So they were technically worshipping God, but not really. They also appointed all sorts of random people as priests to run the rituals at their local shrines. They worshipped God, but they also kept worshipping the old gods from where they came from.
