And they're still doing it today, still worshipping any old god that gives them nostalgic vibes. They don't actually worship the real God—they don't take His commands seriously, the ones He revealed to the children of Jacob, who He renamed Israel. God made a covenant with them and ordered, "Don't worship other gods. Don't serve them, don't sacrifice to them. Worship ME, the God who rescued you from Egypt with my incredible power. Fear me. Worship me. Sacrifice to me. Only me! All the rules I wrote down for you—do them for your whole life. And whatever you do, don't worship other gods! Don't forget the covenant I made with you. And don't worship other gods! Worship God, and only God—He's the one who will save you from your enemies."

But they didn't listen. They just kept doing the same old things. So it turned out, while these people were pretending to worship God, they were also messing with their local idols. And they're still at it. Like father, like son.

title: King Hezekiah's Ultimate Trust Fail

paragraphs: So, in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, who was 25, started ruling Judah. He was king for 29 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah. God actually thought he was a pretty solid king, kinda like his ancestor David. He got rid of all the weird local shrines, smashed these stone pillars people were into, and chopped down the Asherah groves where they were mixing up religion and... other stuff. He even crushed the bronze snake Moses had made way back when, because the Israelites had started sacrificing to it and even gave it a name, Nehushtan, which means 'A Piece of Bronze.' That's kinda creepy.

Hezekiah fully trusted God. Seriously, there was no other king like him, before or after. He stuck with God, never let go, and followed all the rules God gave Moses. And God had his back through everything.

He even rebelled against the king of Assyria and was like, 'Nah, I'm not serving you anymore.' He also pushed the Philistines back, from their sentry outposts to their fortress cities, all the way to Gaza and its borders.

In Hezekiah's fourth year as king—which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel—Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked Samaria and laid siege to it for three years. They finally captured it in Hezekiah's sixth year, which was the ninth year of Hoshea. The king of Assyria then exiled the Israelites, relocating them in Halah, in Gozan and Habor, and in the cities of the Medes.
This all went down because they totally ignored God and didn't care about the promises they made. They just wouldn't listen or do what God's servant Moses had told them.

Fast forward to Hezekiah's fourteenth year as king. Sennacherib, the new king of Assyria, rolled up and captured all of Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah sent a message to the Assyrian king at his headquarters in Lachish, saying, 'My bad, I messed up. Pull your army back, and I'll pay whatever you want.'

The king of Assyria demanded eleven tons of silver and a ton of gold. Hezekiah had to give him all the silver from The Temple of God and the palace. He even stripped the gold from the Temple doors and gave it to the Assyrian king. Wild.

But the king of Assyria still sent his top three military chiefs—the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh—from Lachish with a strong force to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. They stopped by the aqueduct of the Upper Pool and started yelling for King Hezekiah.
Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the royal secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the court historian, went out to meet them.

The third officer, the Rabshakeh, was the spokesman. He said, 'Tell Hezekiah that the great king of Assyria says you're living in a fantasy world. You think just talking about God is a substitute for a real army? You rebelled against my master, so who's gonna help you now? Egypt? They're a joke. And don't give me that 'we trust in God' line. Didn't you just tear down a bunch of his shrines?'

'So, for real, make a deal with my master, the king of Assyria. I'll give you 2,000 horses if you can even find guys to ride them. You can't. So how are you gonna stop even one of my soldiers? You're still hoping for those Egyptian chariots, aren't you? Pathetic.'
'And you think I came here without God's permission? God literally told me to come and destroy this place!'
Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, 'Can you please speak in Aramaic? We understand it. Don't speak in Hebrew, everyone on the city wall can hear you.'
But the Rabshakeh said, 'This message is for everyone. If you guys don't surrender, you'll be eating your own poop and drinking your own pee.' Super gross, right?

Then he yelled in Hebrew so everyone could hear, 'Listen to the king of Assyria! Don't let Hezekiah trick you. He can't save you. Don't listen to his whole 'God will save us' speech. Make a deal with me and you'll live the good life. I'll guarantee every one of you your own plot of ground—a garden and a well! I'll take you to a land sweeter by far than this one, a land of grain and wine, bread and vineyards, olive orchards and honey. You only live once—so live, really live!'

'Don't listen to Hezekiah's lies. Has any god ever saved a nation from the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did the gods of Samaria save them? So what makes you think your God can save Jerusalem from me?'
The people were dead silent. The king had told them not to say a word.

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator, Shebna the royal secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the court historian, tore their clothes and went back to tell Hezekiah everything the Rabshakeh had said.

title: God vs. the Trash-Talking King
paragraphs: When King Hezekiah heard what the messenger said, he totally freaked out and tore his clothes. He put on some really uncomfortable burlap clothes and went straight to God's Temple.
Then he sent his top palace guy, Eliakim, his secretary, Shebna, and the head priests—all wearing the same scratchy burlap—to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
They told Isaiah, "Hezekiah says this is a dark day, a total disaster. It feels like we're about to have a baby but have zero strength to push.

Hopefully, your God heard all the trash talk from the Rabshakeh, sent by the king of Assyria to humiliate the living God. Maybe your God will shut him down. Could you please pray for the people who are left?"
So, that was the message King Hezekiah's crew gave to Isaiah.
Isaiah told them, "Go tell your boss, 'God says: Don't even worry about the garbage you heard from the king of Assyria's suck-up messengers. It's all just talk.'

'Here’s what I'm going to do: I'll afflict him with self-doubt. He'll hear a rumor that makes him run back to his own country scared for his life. And once he's there, I'll make sure he gets taken out.'"

The Rabshakeh left and found that the king of Assyria had pulled up stakes from Lachish and was now fighting against Libnah. Then Sennacherib heard that Tirhakah king of Cush was on his way to fight him. So he sent another message to Hezekiah, saying:

"Don't let your god, the one you trust so much, play you by saying, 'Jerusalem won't fall to the king of Assyria.' That's a straight-up lie. You know my track record—I've destroyed country after country. What makes you think you're special?

Look at all the nations my ancestors wrecked. Did their gods save them? Check out Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden at Tel Assar. All ruins. And what's left of the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, or Ivvah? Just bones."
Hezekiah took the letter, read it, and then went to God's Temple. He spread the letter out right there in front of God. And Hezekiah prayed like he'd never prayed before.

"God of Israel, who sits on a throne above the angels, you are the one and only God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth. Please, God, listen up. Open your eyes and see this. Look at this letter Sennacherib sent, straight-up insulting the living God!

It's true, God. The kings of Assyria have wrecked nations. They burned up their gods in huge bonfires—because they weren't real gods, just statues made of wood and stone. But now, our God, please save us from raw Assyrian power. Make every kingdom on earth know that you are the one and only God."
It wasn't long before Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah.
"God's word: I heard your prayer about King Sennacherib of Assyria. Here's my answer to him:

'The precious city of Jerusalem thinks you're a joke; they're laughing at you behind your back. Who do you think you've been insulting and bad-mouthing? Who do you think you've been flexing on? The Holy One of Israel, that's who!

You sent your little messengers to disrespect the Master. You bragged, ‘With my fleet of chariots, I’ve conquered the highest mountains, even the snowy peaks of Lebanon! I’ve chopped down its best trees. I’ve traveled everywhere, seen the coolest places. I’ve dug wells in the middle of nowhere and drunk foreign water; I’ve walked through the rivers of Egypt.’

Did it ever cross your mind that I'm the one behind all this? I planned this a long, long time ago, and now I'm making it happen. I used you like a weapon to turn proud cities into piles of rocks, leaving their people weak and useless—like weeds, fragile as grass, light as wind-blown chaff.

I know everything you do. I see you when you sit, when you come, and when you go. And yeah, I've seen every single one of your temper tantrums against me. Because of that attitude, that disrespectful, foul temper of yours, I'm putting a hook in your nose and a bit in your mouth and dragging you right back where you came from.'"
"And this, Hezekiah, is the sign that will prove it to you:

This year, you'll eat whatever grows on its own. Next year, you'll eat whatever sprouts up on its own. But in the third year, you'll plant and harvest, grow vineyards and eat grapes. The survivors of Judah will be like a tree that puts down deep roots and produces fruit.
The survivors will come from Jerusalem, from Mount Zion. God's passion will make this happen.
So, here's the bottom line from God about the king of Assyria:

'He won't get into this city. He won't even shoot a single arrow at it. He won't raise a shield against it or build a ramp to attack it. He'll go home the same way he came. He's not getting in. That's God's word! I will protect this city and save it, for my own sake and for my servant David's sake.'"
And that very night, an angel of God came and massacred 185,000 Assyrians. When the people of Jerusalem woke up the next morning, they saw a whole field of dead bodies.

Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, got out of there fast. He went straight home to Nineveh and stayed there. Then one day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his own sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, killed him. They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon became the new king.

title: Hezekiah's Near-Death Experience Was WILD
paragraphs: So, a little while later, Hezekiah got deathly ill. The prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, came to him and was like, “Yo, God says to get your stuff in order, because you’re about to die. You don’t have much time left.”
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to God.
He was like, “Please, God, remember me! Remember how I’ve lived an honest life in front of you, how my heart has been loyal and steady, and how I’ve always tried to do what makes you happy.”
And then he just broke down and cried his eyes out.

Isaiah was on his way out and wasn't even halfway across the courtyard when a message from God stopped him: “Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people, ‘This is a message from God, the God of your ancestor David: I heard your prayer and I saw your tears. I’m going to heal you. In three days, you’ll be walking into God's Temple. I’m adding fifteen years to your life, and I’m protecting you and this city from the king of Assyria. I’m defending this city for my own honor and for my servant David.’'
Then Isaiah said, “Get a plaster of figs and put it on him.”
So they made the fig plaster, put it on his infected sore, and Hezekiah started getting better.
Hezekiah asked Isaiah, “How will I know this is really from God and not just the figs? What’s the sign that God is healing me and that I’ll be walking into the Temple in three days?”
Isaiah said, “This will be your sign from God that he’s gonna do what he promised: Do you want the shadow on the sundial to jump forward ten steps or go backward ten steps? You pick.”
Hezekiah was like, “Making the shadow go forward is easy. Make it go back ten steps.”
So Isaiah prayed to God, and God made the shadow go back ten steps on Ahaz's sundial.

Not long after this, Merodach-baladan, the son of King Baladan of Babylon, heard that Hezekiah had been sick, so he sent him a get-well card and a gift. Hezekiah was super flattered and gave the messengers a full tour of his treasury—the silver, gold, spices, expensive oils, his armory, everything. He showed them all his prized possessions. There wasn't a single thing in his palace or kingdom that Hezekiah didn't show off to them.
Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and asked, “So, what did those guys want? Where’d they come from?”
Hezekiah said, “They came from a country far away—from Babylon.”
“And what did they see in your palace?” Isaiah asked.
“Everything,” said Hezekiah. “I gave them the grand tour. There isn’t anything in my treasury I didn’t show them.”

Then Isaiah told Hezekiah, “Listen to what God has to say about this: A day is coming when everything in your palace, all the stuff your ancestors have collected until now, will be looted and carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, God’s word. And even worse, some of your own sons, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away and made into eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The message from God you’ve given me is good.” But he was lowkey thinking to himself, “Well, at least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.”

The rest of Hezekiah’s story, all his accomplishments, including how he built the reservoir and the tunnel to bring water into the city, are all written down in the official records of the kings of Judah. Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became the next king.

title: Worst King Ever? Manasseh's Messed-Up Reign
paragraphs: So, Manasseh was just twelve when he got the crown, and he reigned in Jerusalem for a wild fifty-five years. His mom's name was Hephzibah. And straight up, in God's eyes, he was a terrible king. Like, seriously evil. He brought back all the gross and corrupt stuff that had been cleaned out of the country when God kicked out the pagan nations for the Israelites. He even rebuilt all the sketchy shrines for sex and religion that his own dad, Hezekiah, had torn down. He made altars and statues for the gross gods Baal and Asherah, just like King Ahab of Israel did. He was super into astrology and worshiping stars, taking his cues from the constellations. He even had the nerve to build these pagan altars right inside God's Temple, the same temple in Jerusalem that God had specifically said was for His name only. He put shrines to the stars in both courtyards of God's Temple. It gets worse—he literally sacrificed his own son by burning him. He was into black magic, fortune-telling, and even held séances to talk to spirits. God saw it as a whole career of doing evil, and He was not happy.

And for the final, most disrespectful move, he put a carved statue of the pagan goddess Asherah right in God's Temple. This was a huge slap in the face to God, who had clearly told David and Solomon, 'In this Temple and in Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, I will put my Name forever. I'll never make my people wander from this land I gave their ancestors again.' But there was a catch: they had to actually follow all the rules He gave them through Moses.
But did the people listen? Nope. Manasseh totally led them astray, and they ended up doing things that were even more evil than the pagan nations God had gotten rid of before.

God was completely done with it all. He sent his prophets to deliver a message: 'Because King Manasseh of Judah has done all these disgusting things, making the sins of the Amorites look like nothing and setting new records for evil, and because he used his nasty idols to turn Judah into a nation of sinners, this is what's going to happen. I, the God of Israel, am bringing a disaster on Jerusalem and Judah so bad that anyone who hears about it will be like, 'No way, I can't even believe that.'

'I'm going to give Jerusalem the same treatment Samaria got, a total repeat of what happened to Ahab. I'm gonna wipe Jerusalem clean like you'd wipe a plate, and then flip it over to dry. I'm ditching what's left of my people and handing them over to their enemies. If their enemies can get anything out of them, good for them. They've been nothing but a headache for me since the day their ancestors left Egypt. They've pushed me to my breaking point, and I'm not putting up with their evil anymore.'

The final verdict on Manasseh was that he was a straight-up murderer who killed indiscriminately. He filled Jerusalem with the blood of innocent people. And that was on top of all the sin he dragged his people into. As far as God was concerned, he turned the whole nation into sinners.

The rest of Manasseh's story, everything he did, and his sad, sinful record are all written down in The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Manasseh died and was buried in the palace garden, the Garden of Uzza. His son Amon became the next king.

Amon was twenty-two when he became king, and he only lasted two years in Jerusalem. His mom was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz from Jotbah. In God's book, he was just as evil as his dad Manasseh. He just copied his father, worshiping the same disgusting gods. He completely bailed on the God of his ancestors and didn't live God's way at all.

Then, Amon's own servants turned on him and assassinated him right in his own palace. But then the people of the land took out the conspirators who killed King Amon and made his son, Josiah, the new king.
The rest of Amon's life is written in The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. They buried him in his tomb in the Garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah took over as king.

title: King Finds Ancient Scroll & Totally Freaks Out
paragraphs: Josiah was just a kid, only eight years old, when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mom was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath. He genuinely tried to live in a way that honored God, following the path of his ancestor David without messing up.

One day, in the eighteenth year of his rule, King Josiah sent his royal secretary, Shaphan son of Azaliah, the son of Meshullam, to the Temple of God. He told him, "Go find Hilkiah the high priest and have him count up all the money that people have donated to the Temple, the cash the doorkeepers have collected. Then, give that money to the project managers overseeing the Temple's renovation. They need to pay the workers—carpenters, builders, and masons. Also, give them the green light to buy lumber and stone for the repairs. Don't even worry about receipts; these guys are all trustworthy."

The high priest Hilkiah told Shaphan, the royal secretary, some major news: "I just found the Book of God's Law, the one that tells us how to live. Found it right here in the Temple!" He handed the scroll to Shaphan, who started reading it.
Shaphan, the secretary, went back to the king to give him the update. "Your crew has gathered all the money from the Temple and handed it over to the foremen to pay the workers," he reported.
Then Shaphan dropped the bombshell: "By the way, Hilkiah the priest gave me a book." And he started reading it out loud to the king.

When the king heard the words from the book, God's own law, he completely lost it and ripped his clothes in distress. He immediately summoned Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Acbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary, and his personal advisor Asaiah. He ordered them, "Go pray to God for me, for the people, for all of Judah! We need to know what to do after hearing what's in this book. God must be seriously furious with us. Our ancestors clearly didn't follow any of the rules in this book, none of the instructions meant for us."

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Acbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went straight to Huldah the prophetess. She was married to Shallum son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, who was in charge of the royal wardrobe, and they lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem. The five men went to consult her. She told them, "This is a message from God, the God of Israel: Go tell the man who sent you that I am about to bring disaster on this place and its people. Every single word written in the book the king of Judah read will come true. Why? Because they've abandoned me for other gods and have made me sick with all their idol-making businesses. My anger is burning white-hot against this place, and no one can stop it.

"But, as for the king of Judah who sent you to ask for God's guidance, tell him this. God's take on the book he read is: 'Because you took the warning of doom seriously, and because you humbled yourself, tore your clothes, and cried before me, I've heard you. This is God's promise: I'll take care of you. You will die in peace and be buried quietly. You won't have to witness the disaster I'm bringing on this place.'"
The men brought her message back to the king.

title: King J's Total Spiritual Reset
paragraphs: The king wasted no time. He got all the leaders from Judah and Jerusalem together. Then, he headed straight for God's Temple with his whole crew—we're talking priests, prophets, and basically everyone, from the honored ones to the nobodies. He then read the entire Book of the Covenant, which they'd found in the Temple, out loud for everyone to hear. The king stood by a pillar and made a serious promise to God. He committed everyone to follow God, obey His rules with all their heart, and actually live out the stuff written in the book. The people were all in, giving a unanimous 'yes.'

Then the king told Hilkiah the high priest and his crew to do a major clean-up of the Temple of God. They had to toss out everything in the Temple of God made for worshiping Baal, Asherah, and all those cosmic powers. He had it all burned outside Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley and got rid of the ashes in Bethel. He fired all the pagan priests the old kings had hired for their local shrines. He basically swept the whole country clean of the nasty stuff associated with the 24/7 worship of Baal, the sun, moon, and stars. He even took the gross Asherah pole from the Temple, burned it in the Kidron Valley, ground it to dust, and scattered the ashes in a public cemetery. He also tore down the rooms in the Temple where male prostitutes worked, which women also used for their weaving projects for Asherah. He got rid of priests from all the towns in Judah and destroyed their shrines from Geba to Beersheba, from one end of the country to the other. He even smashed the shrine at the city gate that was for the private use of the mayor, Joshua. These priests might not have been messing with the main Altar in the Temple, but they were still part of the problem and had to go.

Josiah then wrecked the Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom where people were sacrificing their kids in fire. No more burning sons or daughters for the god Molech. He got rid of the horse statues honoring the sun god that Judah's kings had put up near the entrance to the Temple. They were in the courtyard next to the office of Nathan-Melech, the warden. He burned up the sun-chariots as so much rubbish. Total junk.

The king went on a rampage, smashing all the altars. The ones on the roof shrine of Ahaz, the ones the kings of Judah had built, and the ones Manasseh had put all over the Temple courtyard—he pulverized them all and scattered the dust in the Kidron Valley. He also cleared out all the shrines Solomon had built east of Jerusalem, on the south slope of Abomination Hill, for the gross Sidonian goddess Ashtoreth, the creepy god Chemosh of the Moabites, and the messed-up god Milcom of the Ammonites. He smashed the altars, chopped down the Asherah poles, and threw old bones all over the sites. Next, he went after the altar at the shrine in Bethel that Jeroboam son of Nebat had built—the same Jeroboam who had led Israel into a life of sin. He tore it apart, burned it to ashes, and set the Asherah pole on fire.

While Josiah was looking around, he saw some tombs on a hill. He had the bones taken out and burned on the ruined altars to make them unholy. This was exactly what a man of God had predicted years ago when Jeroboam was standing by that same altar.
Then the king asked, 'Whose memorial stone is that?'
The city guys told him, 'That's the grave of the man of God who predicted all this stuff you're doing to the altar at Bethel.'
Josiah said, 'Leave his bones alone.' So they didn't touch his bones, or the bones of the prophet from Samaria who was buried with him.

But Josiah wasn't done. He went through all the towns in Samaria and destroyed the shrines the kings of Israel had built, the ones that made God so angry. He tore the shrines down and left them in ruins—just as at Bethel. He killed all the priests who worked at those shrines and burned their bodies on their own altars to make them unholy. Only after all that did he go back to Jerusalem.
The king then gave a command to all the people: 'Celebrate the Passover to your God, just like it says in this Book of the Covenant.'

This was a big deal. The Passover hadn't been celebrated like this since the time of the judges—none of the kings of Israel or Judah had done it. But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah's reign, they celebrated this Passover to God in Jerusalem.

Josiah did a total spiritual cleanse. He got rid of all the spirit-mediums, sorcerers, household gods, and idols—all the nasty stuff you could find in Judah and Jerusalem. He did all this in obedience to the words of God's Revelation written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the Temple of God.

There was no king quite like Josiah, before or after him. He turned back to God completely—heart, mind, and soul—and followed all the instructions from Moses. The world would never see another king like him.

But even with all that, God was still furious. His anger, sparked by Manasseh's evil deeds, was still burning. God said, 'I'm going to get rid of Judah just like I got rid of Israel. I'm turning my back on Jerusalem, the city I chose, and this Temple where I said my Name would live.'

The rest of Josiah's story is written in the official records of the kings of Judah. He died when Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt marched out to join forces with the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River. King Josiah tried to stop him at the Plain of Megiddo, but Neco killed him. His servants took his body back to Jerusalem in a chariot and buried him in his own tomb. By popular choice, the people anointed Josiah's son Jehoahaz and made him king after his father.
Jehoahaz was 23 when he became king, but he only lasted for three months in Jerusalem. His mom was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
God's verdict on him? He was an evil king, just like his ancestors.

Pharaoh Neco captured Jehoahaz at Riblah in the country of Hamath and put him in chains so he couldn't rule in Jerusalem. He demanded that Judah pay tribute of nearly four tons of silver and seventy-five pounds of gold. Then Pharaoh Neco put Eliakim, another of Josiah's sons, on the throne and changed his name to Jehoiakim. As for Jehoahaz, he was dragged off to Egypt and died there.
Meanwhile, Jehoiakim acted like a good little puppet and paid the silver and gold Pharaoh demanded. He got the money by taxing the people, forcing everyone to pay up.

Jehoiakim was 25 when he started his rule, and he was king in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Zebidah daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah. And in God's eyes, he was another evil king, following in the footsteps of his ancestors.

title: Judah's Downfall: The Final Betrayal
paragraphs: So, while this dude Jehoiakim was king, the Babylonian king, Nebuchadnezzar, rolled in and took over. Jehoiakim basically became his little puppet. But after three years, he was like, 'Nah, I'm done with this,' and rebelled.

Then God sent a bunch of different crews to mess with him – Babylonian, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiding bands. The whole point was to wreck Judah. God had been warning them this would happen through his prophets, and now it was going down. This wasn't random, either. It was God's judgment because he was so done with Judah after all the messed-up stuff King Manasseh did. That guy was a straight-up killer who had innocent people's blood running in the streets of Jerusalem. God was not going to let that slide.
If you want the full scoop on Jehoiakim, it's all in 'The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.' Anyway, he died and was buried, and his son Jehoiachin took over as king.

Egypt wasn't a problem anymore. Their king wasn't invading because the Babylonian king had already snatched up all the land between the Brook of Egypt and the Euphrates River, which used to be Egypt's turf.

Jehoiachin was 18 when he became king, but he only lasted in Jerusalem for three months. His mom was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan, from Jerusalem. And yeah, God thought he was a bad king too, just like his dad.

The next thing you know, King Nebuchadnezzar's crew attacked Jerusalem and had it surrounded. While they were doing that, Nebuchadnezzar himself showed up. So, King Jehoiachin of Judah, along with his mom, his officials, and all his leaders, just gave up.

In the eighth year of his reign, the king of Babylon took Jehoiachin prisoner. Nebuchadnezzar cleaned out the treasuries of God's Temple and the palace, and he jacked all the gold stuff that King Solomon had made for the Temple. This shouldn't have been a shocker, though—God had said it would happen. Then he kicked a ton of people out of Jerusalem—all the leaders, soldiers, craftsmen, and artisans. He sent like ten thousand of them into exile! The only people left were the super poor.

He dragged Jehoiachin off to Babylon. He also took the king's mom, his wives, his top officials, and all the important people. It was like seven thousand soldiers and a thousand craftsmen and artisans, all forced to move to Babylon.
Then the king of Babylon made Jehoiachin’s uncle, Mattaniah, the new puppet king and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was 21 when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mom was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
As far as God was concerned, Zedekiah was just another bad king, a total copy of Jehoiakim.
All this disaster happened to Jerusalem and Judah because God was so angry. He just turned his back on them. And then, to top it all off, Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

title: The Absolute Worst Ending Ever
paragraphs: So, the revolt dates from the ninth year and tenth month of Zedekiah's reign. King Nebuchadnezzar rolled up to Jerusalem with his entire army, like, no warning. They set up camp and basically trapped everyone inside the city. For 19 months, Jerusalem was on lockdown. By the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, on the ninth day of the month, the hunger was insane. We're talking zero food, not even crumbs. Then, a breakout. At night, under cover of darkness, the entire army escaped through an opening in the wall (it was the gate between the two walls above the King's Garden). They slipped through the lines of the Babylonians who surrounded the city and headed for the Jordan on the Arabah Valley road. But the Babylonians were on them and caught up to King Zedekiah in the Plains of Jericho. By that point, his army had totally bailed on him and scattered. The Babylonians took Zedekiah prisoner and marched him off to the king of Babylon at Riblah, They put him on trial right then and there. And then, the unthinkable: they executed his sons right in front of him. That was the last thing he ever saw, because then they blinded him. They put him in cuffs and shipped him off to Babylon. Wild.

In the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, on the seventh day of the fifth month, His top guy, Nebuzaradan, showed up in Jerusalem. And he went on a rampage. He torched God's Temple, the king's palace, and then the rest of the city. The whole place was literally up in flames. He had his Babylonian soldiers tear down the city walls. Then he rounded up everyone still in the city, even the people who had switched sides to join the Babylonians, and sent them all into exile. He only left a few poor farmers to take care of the vineyards and fields.

The Babylonians broke apart the bronze pillars, the bronze washing stands, and the giant bronze basin from God's Temple and hauled all the bronze to Babylon. They also took all the fancy bronze accessories used in the Temple services, plus the gold and silver incense burners and bowls. The king's deputy didn't leave anything behind—he took every piece of valuable metal he could find.

The amount of bronze they got from the two pillars, the basin, and all the washstands that Solomon had made for God's Temple was insane—they couldn't even weigh it all! Each pillar was 27 feet tall, with another 4.5 feet of fancy bronze designs on top.

The king's deputy also took some important people as prisoners: Seraiah the head priest, Zephaniah the priest under him, three guards, the top army officer left, five of the king's advisors, the accountant, the army's main recruiter, and sixty other important guys from the city. Nebuzaradan, the king's deputy, marched them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And there at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon killed the lot of them in cold blood.
Judah was sent into exile, kicked out of their own land.

As for the regular people left in Judah, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, as governor of them. When the army officers who were still around heard about this, they went to meet Gedaliah at Mizpah. These guys included Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, along with their followers.

Gedaliah promised the officers and their men, 'Don't be scared of the Babylonian officials. Just go back to your farms and families and show respect to the king of Babylon. Trust me, it's all gonna be okay.'

But then, a little while later, in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama (he had royal blood in him), came back with ten men and killed Gedaliah, the Jewish traitors, and the Babylonian officials who were at Mizpah. It was a total bloodbath.
After that, everyone got scared of what the Babylonians would do, so they all dipped and went to Egypt—leaders and regular people, everyone.

Thirty-seven years after King Jehoiachin of Judah was taken into exile, a new king named Evil-Merodach came to power in Babylon and let Jehoiachin out of prison. This happened on the 27th day of the twelfth month. The king was super nice to him and gave him better treatment than any of the other political prisoners in Babylon. Jehoiachin got to take off his prison clothes and ate with the king for the rest of his life. The king gave him everything he needed to live a comfortable life.
